title: Hugh and Mica's Mountain Mission
markdown:
Wizard Hugh lived in a crooked tower that looked as if a giant with a wobbly hand had stuck it on the jagged Whispering Mountains. Thin crisp air tickled his nose: sleepy pines, and the faint fizz of spells not quite finished. Down in the valley, lanterns on sturdy ropes cast a dancing warm glow over paths only the bravest goats dared.

Hugh’s beard was as tangled as a rabbit’s favourite hiding place, brown and grey. His robes wore a sprinkle of glitter he called accidental sparkles. He clutched a small soft box of deep purple velvet: the Parcel of Perpetual Pondering. It had to reach the Elder of the Sunstone Valley before the last sliver of moon winked out.

“Hurry now, Mica, my little scaly friend.” Spectacles up, as crooked as the tower. “Time is rushing faster than a sneeze on a windy day. If the Elder doesn’t get this on time, he might ponder until the whole valley starts asking why about everything. Head-scratching for weeks.”

Mica, a gecko with emerald scales like a treasure chest of jewels, clung to his shoulder, sticky claws like tiny suction cups. A soft encouraging chirp, a tiny bell.

Hugh set off, worn boots on a goat track that dipped and swerved like a playful snake. He hummed: his organised mind sorting routes. Reliable spells in a pocket. A map on a napkin so crisp it crinkled. A canvas bag of emergency biscuits. A wizard never knew.

The track narrowed where meltwater had undercut the stones. Hugh paused, one boot hovering, and consulted the napkin. The ink had run at a fold, so the path looked like a squiggle arguing with itself. Mica chirped once, as if to say the mountain did not care about napkins.

The sun, a cheerful orange ball, painted fiery orange, soft pink, dreamy violet. Hugh stopped. “Now, let me think.” A thoughtful tap on velvet. “How to make this delivery legendary? Dragon’s breath to clear the path? Too smoky, everyone coughing. A chariot of six leaping squirrels? Exciting, but the paperwork—squirrel tail maintenance, acorns for payment. Or a magnificent swirling vortex of stardust? Splendid.”

He pictured himself arriving in a glitter of cosmic dust, the valley gasping, the Elder impressed. The picture was so fine he nearly missed a loose pebble rolling toward the ravine.

Mica flicked a long pink tongue: not entirely convinced. She nudged his ear with a tiny cool snout.

Hugh sighed, beard ruffling. “But Mica, that hardly sounds legendary. The valleys expect pizzazz. A touch of the truly extraordinary.” He peered into a shadowy ravine. Cold air rose from it, smelling of wet stone and last year’s pine needles. “Slide down a shimmering rainbow? Then how would I climb back?”

Mica chirped, more determined, and pointed her delicate nose at a narrow ledge barely visible against grey rock: too small for a rainbow, too steep for leaping squirrels.

“That’s just a little ledge. Perfectly practical, of course, but not magical enough for a delivery of this importance.”

Without another chirp she hopped to a sturdy rock, stretched her slender emerald body, flicked her tail, and scurried onto the ledge. Silent grace. Tiny feet found bumps and cracks Hugh could not see. She disappeared around a rocky bend.

Hugh’s jaw hung. His small quiet gecko was navigating the path he had dismissed as not magical enough, with an ease he had never witnessed. No rainbows. No stardust. Climbing. And heading exactly toward Sunstone Valley.

He tucked the napkin map into a pocket. It had not mentioned the ledge. It had mentioned, in his own neat handwriting, *vortex optional*.

“Wait for me!” Understanding dawned. His organised brain, nudged by a remarkably sensible companion, saw it: practicality was not always flashy. It was often the most reliable way. He had been so busy looking for big magic he had missed simple clever skill. Mica was not using spells. She was using gecko talents, which was just as powerful.

He scrambled after, wizardly boots clumsy on the tiny ledge, a wry smile. “Perhaps the legend will be about the wizard who almost tumbled off a cliff, cleverly guided by his exceptionally sensible gecko. A good punchline.”

The velvet box bumped his ribs. He held it tighter. Below, the ravine made a sound like a long slow swallow. Hugh did not look down again. He looked at Mica’s tail, a green comma against the grey, and put his boot where her feet had already voted.

Mica waited at a wider section, bright intelligent eyes encouraging. Together they went, her small shimmering form a beacon of quiet determination, master of the mountain path. Once Hugh’s boot slipped; Mica froze, then tapped the rock twice, as if to scold it. He found a better hold. Accidental sparkles drifted off his sleeve and vanished into the dusk.

As the last sliver of moon cast a pale pearly gleam, they arrived at the Elder’s cozy cottage in the heart of Sunstone Valley. Smoke from the chimney smelled of bread. A hedgehog on the doorstep considered them, then considered a leaf, then considered them again.

The Elder, a kindly old woman whose smile was as warm as freshly baked bread, accepted the Parcel. “Oh, Hugh. Nick of time. I was starting to wonder if I’d send search parties of very confused hedgehogs.”

Hugh, breathless, beaming, looked at Mica on his shoulder. “All thanks to Mica’s legendary climbing skills.” A twinkle.

The Elder did not open the box. She set it on a shelf beside a kettle and a stack of unanswered questions, and that seemed to be enough.

Back in the village: spiced cider in steaming mugs, a storyteller of brave goats and clever foxes. Hugh and Mica found a spot by a crackling fire. The parcel delivered, moonrise met. Accidental sparkles still on the robes. He offered Mica a crumb of emergency biscuit. She took it as if she had earned the whole bag.

The valley, for the moment, did not have to ask why.
audience: children aged 9-10, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for independent readers
